description: Authored map for the admission of the risk-debate candidate pack (research/risk-debate) by scripts/risk-debate-admission.ts. It applies the maintainer's decisions of 2026-10-30 (open questions 1–15, all as recommended) and the adjudication of 2026-10-31 of the cross-family check, both recorded in review/risk-debate-pack-2026-10-29.md. Every decision, correction and hold here carries its reason. Records not named here are admitted as the pack states them, under the general rules in `rules`.
snapshotDescription: Rows added and changed by the admission of the risk-debate candidate pack (scripts/risk-debate-admission.ts, review/risk-debate-admission-2026-10-31.md). Removing the added rows and restoring the changed ones reproduces the dataset as it was at baseCommit.
scope: The risk-debate admission (2026-10-31) adds the collection of arguments about catastrophic risk from advanced AI, 2000–2026: published texts that state, contest or bear on sixteen propositions of their own and on the existing treacherous-turn and fast-takeoff propositions, with the published replies between them; every record is a seed with machine-checked evidence.
rules: Decision 1: the pack's R04 records are admitted on the existing concept treacherous-turn (B1) and its R05 records on fast-or-hard-takeoff (A4), each classified against that concept's own criterion; the pack's earliest-located roles on R04 and R05 lapse, and B1 and A4 keep the roles their collection decided. The superintelligence collection names no earliest-located contesting record, so no admitted record takes that role on B1 or A4.
Decision 1, IDs: the pack's working codes R04 and R05 are re-lettered in record IDs (rd-r04- to rd-b1-, rd-r05- to rd-a4-), as the ontology asks for working codes (schema 2.22).
Convention C4: admitted proposition-record IDs are stance-neutral. The pack's suffixes -contests and -context are dropped unless that would give two records one ID.
Decision 2: R03 is admitted as its own concept, inner-or-deceptive-misalignment; no text recorded on B3 or B4 is re-recorded on it.

Decision 3: the Yudkowsky claims Y02, Y09, Y11, Y13, Y15, Y19 and Y20 stay separate; each is linked to its R counterpart in both collection definitions (src/reading/risk-debate.ts and src/reading/yudkowsky-arguments.ts), and B3 and B4 to R03 in the superintelligence definition.
Decisions 4 and 5: R10a, R10b and the narrowed R13 and R14 criteria are admitted as the pack states them.
Decisions 11–13: the 2019 thread records are dated by the compiler's copy; reports and signed statements are recorded as texts, with no stance attributed to any signatory and no signatory list.
Decision 14: the pack's 22 replies are admitted as cites claims with the reply qualification; its 17 debates become a reading list in the collection definition, not a schema type.
Decision 15: no record or interface text places a record or an author on a side; the pack's position counts stay in the research files.

No schema change: the pack's `comparative` attribute (R08/R09 ranking) has no schema field and is not admitted; the two records that rank misuse above loss of control say so in their statements already. Its date bases `posting`, `submission` and `delivery` become `publication` (posting and submission, with the basis in the note) or no basis (delivery, a talk).
Adjudication of 2026-10-31: earlier-located roles move only to dated texts; leads whose historical date cannot be pinned are listed in the collection's search note, not admitted as headlines.
Reader-facing text never names a record ID; a pointer to another record becomes "recorded separately".

R03.note: Decision 2: B3 (deceptive alignment) and B4 (scheming) are narrower cases; texts recorded on them are not re-recorded here.

R10a.reason: The pack's working ID (intelligence-brings-benevolence-risk-debate) names the collection; the admitted ID names the proposition and does not collide with Y02's intelligence-brings-benevolence.

newClaims.subject: joy-2000-why-the-future
newClaims.statement: Joy's essay of April 2000 argues that robotics, genetic engineering and nanotechnology could make humans an endangered species, and asks whether, if extinction is a likely or even possible outcome of technological development, we should not proceed with great caution.

time.note: Wired, issue of April 2000; the page dates it 1 April 2000.

newClaims.qualification: Joy treats intelligent robots alongside genetic engineering and nanotechnology, not AI alone, and argues for limiting the development of dangerous technologies. Quotations in the essay from a 1995 manifesto keep that earlier date and are not used here. Earliest located among the texts the searches found, after a cross-family check located it; it is not evidence of coinage.

evidence.passage: Our most powerful 21st-century technologies—robotics, genetic engineering, and nanotech—are threatening to make humans an endangered species.
evidence.note: The deck is the magazine's summary of the essay; the essay's own wording is in the next passage.

evidence.locator: Paragraph before the section on the dream of robotics, closing question
evidence.passage: And if our own extinction is a likely, or even possible, outcome of our technological development, shouldn’t we proceed with great caution?
evidence.note: Added at admission so that the record rests on the author's own words; not part of the cross-family check's selection.

newClaims.reason: Adjudication of 2026-10-31: Joy (April 2000) earliest located on R07 (check item 7).

newClaims.subject: goertzel-2002-thoughts-on-ai-morality

newClaims.qualification: The essay states the difficulty as an objection to one proposed design (Yudkowsky's), not as an impossibility result. Earliest located among the texts the searches found, after a cross-family check located it; it is not evidence of coinage.

evidence.locator: Section 1, discussion of Yudkowsky's proposed architecture
evidence.passage: very unlikely to succeed at producing an AGI value system that is robust enough to survive successive, drastic intelligence-increase-directed self-modifications.

newClaims.subject: goertzel-2004-positive-transcension
newClaims.statement: Goertzel's essay of 17 February 2004 attributes the scenario of a dominating AI to anthropomorphism and states that making such an AI would probably require explicitly programming it with a lust for power.
newClaims.qualification: A conditional claim that a drive to dominate would not arise by default, not a claim that intelligence brings benevolence. Earliest located among the texts the searches found, after a cross-family check located it; it is not evidence of coinage.

evidence.locator: Section 2.9, discussion of the Megalomaniac AI scenario
evidence.passage: in order to make a Megalomaniac AI, one would probably need to explicitly program an AI with a lust for power.

newClaims.subject: corrigibility-2015
newClaims.statement: Soares, Fallenstein, Yudkowsky and Armstrong's paper of January 2015 states that rational agents have default incentives to resist being shut down or having their preferences modified, and that simple attempts to define a utility function that removes those incentives prove unsatisfactory.

time.note: Workshop dates of 25–26 January 2015 in the header of the PDF.

engagement.rationale: It disputes the premise that ordinary engineering can give a capable agent objectives that leave it open to shutdown and correction.

newClaims.qualification: A technical argument about a formal shutdown problem, not a proof that control is impossible; the paper presents its failed proposals as pointing to further research.
